_how: The editor writes one piece a day: stories on even days, spices on odd days, from the top of each list, then moves it to done with the date. Jacqueline or the editor may add, reorder or cut. Recipes are never written by the editor: they go to recipes_for_zahra.

stories.angle: The shared dish: eating from your own triangle of the tagine, the host pushing the best pieces to the guest, why one plate makes people slow down. Blends: chermoula, sweet-tagine.
Breaking the fast at sunset: dates, harira, chebakia, the silence then the noise. The rhythm of a whole month of eating at the sun's hours. Blends: golden-hour, sweet-tagine.
The neighbourhood ferran: children carrying trays of dough through the derb, each loaf marked, the baker who knows every family's bread. Blends: kemoun, moroccan-zaatar.
Tanjia: the clay urn of meat cooked all day in the ashes of a hammam furnace, Marrakech's dish of working men. Blends: ras-el-hanout, taliouine-saffron.
Msemen, baghrir, olive oil, amlou, mint tea: a Moroccan breakfast as a lesson in not hurrying. Blends: golden-hour, spiced-coffee.
Pastilla, mechoui, lamb with prunes: the dishes of celebration and the women who cook them for two hundred. Blends: sweet-tagine, kemoun.
The pause after the long lunch: shutters half closed, the house slows, tea again. Why the middle of the day belongs to rest. Blends: dusk, a-whole-day.
The couscoussier and the gsaa: who makes the clay and wooden tools of couscous (UNESCO names potters and family workshops), and why a dish needs its own pot. Blends: ras-el-hanout.
The white cone of sugar: the little hammer, the lidded box, two loaves carried to a marriage proposal, and Morocco's Saadian sugar mills of the sixteenth century. Blends: sweet-tagine, spiced-coffee.
The attar of Souk el-Attarine: one seller for scent and spice together, rose buds beside cloves, amber beside cinnamon; the word that gave English attar of roses. Blends: ras-el-hanout, dusk.

spices.angle: Kasbour seed: citrusy, nutty, the quiet half of so many blends. Blends: chermoula, ras-el-hanout, dry-harissa.
Qaqula: the green pod in coffee and in a good ras el hanout; how it travelled from India. Blends: spiced-coffee, golden-hour, ras-el-hanout.
Zaatar in Morocco: the wild thyme and oregano of the mountains, in tea, on bread with oil. Blends: moroccan-zaatar.
Dried red chilli and harissa in Morocco: gentler than Tunisia, served on the side. Blends: dry-harissa, chermoula.
Dried damask rose buds from the Valley of Roses near Kelaat M'Gouna, in ras el hanout and pastries. Blends: ras-el-hanout.
Louiza: the herb Moroccans steep after dinner. Blends: dusk.
Elbezar: the pepper that travelled the caravan routes, in nearly every Moroccan blend. Blends: golden-hour, ras-el-hanout.
Gouza and bsibsa: one fruit, two spices, sweet tagines and ras el hanout. Blends: sweet-tagine, spiced-coffee, ras-el-hanout.
White pepper beside the black: the softer heat in a pale chicken tagine with olives and lemon, no dark flecks in the sauce. Blends: golden-hour, ras-el-hanout.
Karwiya: the seed in harissa, cousin of cumin and often mistaken for it. Blends: dry-harissa.
